item.title: Absolutism after 1848 (Habsburg)
item.description: Absolutism after 1848 (Habsburg) Absolutismus (“absolutism”) is the word Friedjung and Springer use for the monarchical course in the Habsburg lands after the defeat of the revolutions of 1848–49: government without a working representative constitution, the March constitution of 1849 abandoned, and...

item.title: Bach system
item.description: Bach system The Bachsche System (DE Bachsche System (“Bach system”)) is the name, fixed in Friedjung’s history and in common political speech, for the absolutist (after 1848) interior regime associated with Alexander Bach after the defeat of the 1848–49 revolutions: bureaucratic centralisation, Germ...

item.title: Bonapartism
item.description: Bonapartism Bonapartism in these deposits is the political force that treated the Napoleonic name as a popular and military title to rule France after Waterloo—distinct from legitimism, from Orléanist parliamentary culture, and from republican socialism.

item.title: Burschenschaften
item.description: Burschenschaften Burschenschaften are the German student associations of the post-1815 generation that Treitschke’s Deutsche Geschichte treats as youthful carriers of national and liberal agitation inside the German Confederation—watched, restricted, and partly broken by Bund and Austrian-led police...

item.title: Carbonari (Carboneria)
item.description: Carbonari (Carboneria) The Carboneria (“charcoal-burners’ society”; members Carbonari) was the chief Italian secret society of the Restoration decades before young-italy.

item.title: Charte constitutionnelle
item.description: Charte constitutionnelle The Charte constitutionnelle is the constitutional text of Restoration and July Monarchy France—1814’s granted charter and 1830’s revision—through which Duvergier’s parliamentary history reads every cabinet fight of the Bourbon and Orléanist decades.

item.title: Concert of Europe
item.description: Concert of Europe The Concert of Europe names the post-1815 practice by which the great powers—above all the victors of 1814–15—claimed a shared right to manage crises, congresses, and interventions so that no single revolution or conquest would again overturn the continental order.

item.title: Doctrinaires
item.description: Doctrinaires The doctrinaires (“Doctrinaires”) were the small but influential constitutional group of the French Restoration who sought a middle way between ultra-royalism and pure liberal opposition, grounding the Charte in a theory of representation, capacity, and strong but lawful government.
